record.text: PHP2Shell Vulnerability Gets a Public PoC Exploit for Security Testing

external.description:
A public proof-of-concept repository shares verification tools and a lab setup to test two critical PHP vulnerabilities known as php2shell. The flaws, tracked by researchers as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, are reported to affect PHP’s session.upload_progress feature and could lead to remote code execution under certain conditions. 



 The release adds technical detail to a fast-moving security issue. PHP’s security team announced that an emergency release would address two critical vulnerabilities, each rated 9.2 under CVSS v4.0, and urged users to prepare to upgrade. 



 Its notice scheduled the release for October 21 at 14:00 UTC. At the time of writing, that release time has not yet passed, so PHP’s official notice has not confirmed the technical details, affected versions or fixed builds described in the research repository. 



 The repository says the vulnerabilities affect PHP versions 5.4.0 through 8.5.11. It lists PHP 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27 and 8.5.12 as planned fixed versions, but administrators should verify these against the PHP team’s release advisory before updating. The PHP project’s advance notice confirms the severity and planned release, but not those version details. 



 PHP2Shell Vulnerability PoC Exploit 



 The researcher’s write-up describes several paths to code execution, rather than one universal exploit that works against every PHP website. One chain combines session-file injection with a local file inclusion flaw in an application. 



 According to the repository, this path depends on upload progress being enabled and an application flaw that allows a local file to be included. A local file inclusion bug occurs when an application can be made to load a file from its server in an unintended way. 



 The repository says PHP’s upload-progress handler stores a supplied filename in session data without validating it. It also reports that a session identifier sent in a POST body can bypass the session.use_only_cookies setting, which is meant to restrict how session IDs are accepted. 



 These claims describe how a weakness in PHP’s session handling could combine with a separate application bug. They should not be taken to mean that every PHP site is immediately exploitable through this route. 



 A second reported issue involves a use-after-free, a memory error that can occur when software continues to use data after it has been released. The researcher says that re-entry into a var_destroy destructor can trigger this condition and reports confirming it with AddressSanitizer, a tool used to find memory errors. 



 The repository also describes a PHP-FPM serializer state that may persist across requests, and a handler mismatch that may cause a destructor to run after deserialization fails. The researchers say some of these paths need additional conditions, such as an application gadget or access to a local file. 



 These technical claims remain those of the independent research project until they can be compared with PHP’s full advisory and patches. Security teams should avoid treating every listed path as independently confirmed for all versions or configurations. The project’s verification repository provides the research overview and lab files. Its stated purpose is controlled testing, not use against systems without permission. 



 PHP runs a wide range of websites and applications, so a flaw in its core session handling could affect many types of deployments. The risk can be greater when an application already has a file inclusion weakness or unsafe deserialization behavior. 



 As previous PHP security coverage has shown, memory errors in PHP components can have a serious impact, though the technical causes differ. This report also covers another example of application-level risk on ScriptCase vulnerabilities . 



 The reported score of 9.2 signals a critical issue, but it does not tell administrators whether a particular server is exposed. That depends on the PHP version, configuration, application behavior, and whether the necessary conditions for a specific chain exist. The public repository includes a PHP-FPM and Nginx lab for testing. Organizations should use such environments only for authorized validation and should not run proof-of-concept code against production systems. 



 Administrators should inventory PHP installations across web servers, containers and managed hosting environments, then check the official PHP security release for confirmed affected and fixed versions. Once a suitable update is available, apply it promptly and restart PHP-FPM or the relevant web service so the new binaries take effect. 



 Systems running end-of-life PHP branches require special attention because they may not receive official fixes. The repository identifies PHP 5.x, 7.x, 8.0 and 8.1 as unsupported, but teams should confirm support status with the PHP project. 



 The researcher lists disabling session.upload_progress and setting session.use_only_cookies to On as temporary safeguards. These settings may reduce exposure to some reported paths, but the repository warns that they do not address every attack chain. 



 They are not a substitute for a security update. Review applications for local file inclusion and unsafe deserialization issues, and check server logs for unusual requests involving PHP session handling while the official advisory is being reviewed. 



 For now, the public proof-of-concept is best treated as a signal to prepare and validate safely. The key next step is to compare the research claims with PHP’s official release details, then patch affected systems as soon as the project publishes confirmed fixed versions.

record.text: Microsoft Offers $40,000 for Complete Azure Vulnerability Reports, Just $4,000 for Incomplete Ones

external.description:
Microsoft has introduced a new report-assessment system across its bug bounty programs , making the evidence security researchers submit a key factor in their rewards. 



 Under the Azure bounty program, eligible critical remote code execution and privilege escalation reports can earn $40,000 when assessed as Complete, compared with $4,000 when marked Not Complete. 



 The change applies to reports submitted from October 20, 2026, at 8 AM Pacific Time. Earlier submissions remain subject to the previous report quality requirements. 



 Microsoft says the update aims to reduce requests for missing details and help its security teams reproduce and assess vulnerabilities faster. 



 The $40,000 figure is not a standard payment for every Azure vulnerability . Microsoft’s Azure Bounty Program ties awards to security impact, severity, and report completeness. 



 Microsoft Offers $40,000 for Complete Azure Vulnerability Reports 



 Critical information disclosure reports carry general awards of $12,000 when complete and $1,200 when incomplete. Critical spoofing and tampering reports qualify for $8,000 or $800, respectively. 



 Important remote code execution reports can receive $30,000 when complete, against $3,000 when incomplete. Azure’s published award range remains $400 to $60,000, with additional rewards possible at Microsoft’s discretion. Certain high-impact scenarios also carry percentage increases. 



 A complete report does not automatically qualify for payment or make a vulnerability critical. Microsoft assesses severity and security impact separately. Azure submissions must also meet program rules, including demonstrating an eligible issue on the latest, fully patched service or product. 



 Microsoft expects clear reproduction steps, a reliable proof of concept, the vulnerability type, and accurate technical analysis. Researchers must identify the affected environment, relevant versions, attack requirements, and what an attacker could achieve. They should explain the root cause where possible. 


 
 Azure bounty rewards depend on report completeness (source : Microsoft) 
 


 The key test is whether an engineer unfamiliar with the finding can reproduce and assess it using the initial submission. Missing a required detail or supporting file can result in a Not Complete assessment, even if Microsoft later requests more information. 



 Evidence requirements depend on the vulnerability. Memory corruption reports may need crash data, call stacks, and proof-of-concept source code. 



 File redirection findings may require Process Monitor logs, while NTLM coercion or relay reports may need packet captures. Web application findings can require videos and scripts. 



 Researchers must enter reproduction steps and technical details directly into the MSRC Researcher Portal fields. An attached document does not replace those entries. Microsoft’s report completeness guidance explains the required evidence. 



 Microsoft says AI-assisted research makes it easier to submit potential findings at scale. It welcomes AI use, but reports must still contain accurate analysis and evidence that demonstrates the issue. 



 Previous reporting on Azure application spoofing flaws shows why the exact bypass matters. Researchers demonstrated how invisible Unicode characters could defeat restrictions on reserved application names. 



 Coverage of a Microsoft authentication flaw also illustrates the link between research, disclosure, and remediation. After receiving the report, Microsoft restricted the affected endpoint and awarded the researcher $5,000. 



 For researchers, the practical change is that documentation now carries a clear financial consequence. A valid finding needs a reproducible demonstration, supported technical claims, and the required files from the start. Testing must still stay within Microsoft’s rules rather than exceed permitted access simply to prove greater impact.

Steven Swinford - Political Editor, Patrick Maguire- Chief Political Commentator , Eleanor Hayward - Health Editor
Shabana Mahmood is fighting a rearguard action to save her migration reforms in the face of mounting public criticism from cabinet colleagues.

The home secretary is under pressure to water down plans that would make it harder for foreign workers to claim permanent residence.

Andy Burnham is considering exempting care workers from a proposal to extend the qualifying period for claiming indefinite leave to remain (ILR) from five years to 15.

However, the Home Office has argued that the move could lead to an exodus of foreign care workers from their jobs once they gained permanent residence and were no longer bound by the terms of their visas. An ally of Mahmood said she retained Burnham’s broad support for the plans: “Andy has been on Shabana’s side throughout this row over ILR. He is holding the line.”

Scholarly concern with intent re ects a crucial question for labeling events “genocide”: namely, whether group annihilatio n is the primary objective or overall design of a campaign of violence. But the term “intent” arguably has two limitations for social research. First, “intent” usually refers to individuals and to the contents of their thought, re ecting a legal concern with individua l criminality. “Intent” does not characterize actions by regimes or states. Second, intent may be dif cult to demonstrate where no proof of thought exists. An annihilatio n campaign might be evident, even though intent is never publicly declared or recorded. Given these concerns, a preferable term to designate genocide’s speci city might be “organized” as in “organized group annihilation” or “organized attempt to annihilate a group.” Organization implies that annihilatio n is a killing campaign’s objective, but the term focuses attention at an aggregate regime or institutiona l level rather than at an individual level. Thought need not be demonstrated ; rather, the research question is whether annihilatio n was planned , coordinated , systematic, patterned , and, above all, carried out.
